name: 2 Samuel
author: The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition credited the prophets Samuel, Nathan and Gad, though Samuel dies before these events begin. Many scholars think it was put together later, perhaps around the time of the exile in Babylon (500s BC), by writers who wove older court records and stories into one long history of Israel. Others hold that much of it was written much earlier, close to David's own time. 1 and 2 Samuel were originally a single book.
audience: It was first written for the people of Israel, especially those who cared about King David and his royal family line. If the book reached its final form around the exile, its first readers had lost their land, temple and king, and were looking back on how their kingdom began.
era: The events cover David's reign, around 1010 to 970 BC. Israel's twelve tribes were only loosely joined, and the Philistines, a powerful people on the coast, were a constant threat. David united the tribes, made Jerusalem his capital, and fought neighbouring peoples such as the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites and Arameans. Kings in the region kept large households with several wives, and fights over who would inherit the throne were common.

notes.1:17: This lament is said to come from the Book of Jashar, an ancient collection of Israelite poems and songs that has since been lost.
notes.2:1: Hebron, an old town in the hills of Judah, was linked with Abraham's family burial place and became David's first capital.
notes.2:12: Archaeologists have uncovered a large rock-cut pool at el-Jib, north of Jerusalem, which is often linked with the pool of Gibeon.
notes.5:6: Jerusalem was held by the Jebusites, a Canaanite people. It sat on the border between the tribes of Benjamin and Judah, and the Israelites had never managed to drive the Jebusites out.
notes.6:1: The ark was a gold-covered chest holding the covenant stone tablets; it had stayed at Kiriath Jearim, here called by its other name, Baale Judah, for years after the Philistines returned it.
notes.8:15: This passage lists David's chief officials. Among them, the Kerethites and Pelethites were probably foreign soldiers serving as the king's bodyguard, possibly with links to Crete and the Philistines.
notes.11:1: Spring, after the winter rains, was the usual season for war; Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, lies under modern Amman in Jordan.
notes.21:1: Many scholars see chapters 21–24 as a collection of extra stories, lists and poems, not in time order; the Gibeonites were Canaanites protected by an old treaty.
notes.22:1: This song appears again, almost word for word, as Psalm 18, whose heading also links it to David's rescue from Saul and his enemies.
notes.24:18: The later book of 2 Chronicles names this threshing floor, an open flat area for separating grain, as the place where Solomon built the temple.
